chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from Al-Fadl ibn Shazan, from Ibn Abi Umayr, and Safwan ibn Yahya, from Muawiya ibn Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Perform Tawaf around the House (Kaaba) seven circuits, and say during the Tawaf: 'O Allah! I ask You by Your Name by which one walks upon the surface of the water just as one walks upon the hard ground. And I ask You by Your Name by which Your Throne shakes, and I ask You by Your Name by which the feet of Your Angels shake.'

And I ask You by Your Name by which Musa (peace be upon him) called upon You from the side of Mount Tur, so You answered him and cast love upon him from Yourself. And I ask You by Your Name by which You forgave Muhammad (peace be upon him and his family) whatever of his sin had preceded and whatever had followed, and You completed Your favor upon him, that You do with me such and such, whatever You please of the supplication.

And every time you reach the Door of the Kaaba, send blessings upon the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family). And say in what is between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone: 'Our Lord! Grant us good in the world and good in the Hereafter, and save us from the punishment of the Fire.'
And say during the Tawaf: 'O Allah! I am needy to You, and I am fearful seeking refuge, so do not change my body nor replace my name.'
ai.seo_question: What are the recommended supplications to recite while performing Tawaf around the Kaaba?
ai.summary: This hadith from Al-Kafi details the ritual supplications for Tawaf, emphasizing the power of Allah's Names through cosmic imagery, such as the trembling of the Throne and the steps of angels. It uniquely integrates historical prophetic references—specifically Musa at Mount Tur and Muhammad’s forgiveness—to ground the supplicant's plea in established divine mercy. The text also prescribes specific prayers at the Door of the Kaaba and between the Yemeni Corner and Black Stone, reflecting the Shia tradition of combining physical ritual with deep theological reflection.
